concepts.name: `heapq` keeps a min-heap in a plain list
Top-k with a heap of size k

questions.prompt: Starting from `h = []`, you call `heapq.heappush(h, x)` for `x` in `5, 1, 8, 3`, in that order. What is `h` afterwards?
questions.explanation: A heap is not a sorted list. `heapq` only keeps `heap[k] <= heap[2*k+1]` and `heap[k] <= heap[2*k+2]`. Pushing 5, 1 and 8 gives `[1, 5, 8]`. Then 3 is appended at index 3, whose parent is index 1 (5), so the two swap: `[1, 3, 8, 5]`. The smallest item is always at index 0, but the rest is only partly ordered.

questions.prompt: `h` is a non-empty list that `heapq` functions maintain. Which statement is always true?

choices.text: `h[0]` is the smallest item
`h[-1]` is the largest item
`h` is sorted in ascending order
`h[1]` is the second-smallest item

questions.explanation: `heapq` is a min-heap: every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the root, `h[0]`, is the smallest item. Nothing more is guaranteed. The largest item can be any leaf, not only the last one, and the second smallest can be `h[1]` or `h[2]`, because both are children of the root.

questions.prompt: You have a list of n scores and want a heap of them. What do `heapq.heapify(scores)` and n separate `heappush` calls into an empty list each cost?

choices.text: Both are O(n log n)
`heapify` is O(n); n pushes are O(n log n)
`heapify` is O(n log n); n pushes are O(n)
Both are O(n)

questions.explanation: The `heapq` docs say `heapify` transforms a list into a heap in place, in linear time. Each `heappush` costs O(log n), because the new item can move up the whole height of the tree, so n pushes cost O(n log n). When you already have all the items, call `heapify` once.

questions.prompt: What does `heapq.heappop(h)` cost on a heap of n items, and why?

choices.text: O(1), because the smallest item is already at `h[0]`
O(n), because removing index 0 shifts every other item left
O(n log n), because the rest of the list has to be re-sorted
O(log n), because the last item moves to the root and sifts down the tree

questions.explanation: Reading `h[0]` is O(1), but popping it must restore the heap. `heappop` moves the last item to the root and swaps it down past smaller children, at most the height of the tree, which is about log n levels. It never shifts the whole list the way `list.pop(0)` does.

questions.prompt: From a list of a million prices you need, on different days: the single highest price, the 5 highest, and the 900,000 highest. Which tool do you use for each, and why?

model_answer.summary: Use `max()` for one item, `heapq.nlargest` (a small heap) for a few, and `sorted()` when you need most of the list, as the `heapq` docs advise.
key_points: For the single highest, `max()` is best: one O(n) pass, and the docs say to use `min()`/`max()` when n is 1
For the top 5, `heapq.nlargest(5, prices)` keeps a heap of size 5: about O(n log k) time and O(k) extra memory
For the top 900,000, `sorted(prices, reverse=True)[:900_000]` is better: the docs say `nlargest` is best for small n and `sorted()` is more efficient for larger values
The heap only pays off when k is much smaller than the number of items

questions.explanation: A heap of size k costs O(log k) per item, so it beats sorting only when k is small compared with n. When k is close to n, the heap does nearly as much work as a sort with more overhead, and when k is 1 a plain scan is enough.

questions.prompt: Kth Largest Element in a Stream: `KthLargest(3, [4, 5, 8, 2])` keeps a min-heap of the 3 largest values seen so far. Then you call `add(3)`, `add(5)` and `add(10)`. What does `add(10)` return?
questions.explanation: The heap starts as {4, 5, 8}. `add(3)` pushes 3 and pops it straight back out (it is the smallest), so the heap is still {4, 5, 8} and it returns 4. `add(5)` pops 4, leaving {5, 5, 8}. `add(10)` pops a 5, leaving {5, 8, 10}, and the root, 5, is the 3rd largest. 10 is the largest, not the 3rd largest.

questions.prompt: You find the k largest of n numbers by keeping a min-heap of at most k items and replacing the root whenever a bigger number arrives. What are the time and extra space costs?

choices.text: O(n log k) time and O(k) extra space
O(k log n) time and O(n) extra space
O(n log n) time and O(k) extra space
O(n + k) time and O(1) extra space

questions.explanation: Each of the n numbers costs at most one push or replace on a heap that never holds more than k items, so O(log k) each and O(n log k) in total. The heap is the only extra memory, so O(k). O(n log n) is what a full sort costs, and the heap beats it when k is small.

questions.prompt: Implement top-k (the k largest numbers) with a heap of size k, in words or code, and state its complexity. Why is it a min-heap even though you want the largest numbers?

model_answer.summary: Keep a min-heap of the k largest numbers seen so far; its root is the smallest of them, so it is the one to evict when a bigger number arrives. It runs in O(n log k) time and O(k) space.
key_points: Push numbers until the heap holds k items
For each later number, if it is bigger than the root `h[0]`, replace the root (`heapreplace` or `heappushpop`); otherwise skip it
A min-heap is used because its root is the smallest of the current top k, which is exactly the item to throw out
Time is O(n log k) and extra space O(k), better than sorting's O(n log n) when k is small
It works on a stream, because it never needs all n numbers in memory at once

questions.explanation: The trick is that the heap holds the answer so far, and the only question for each new number is whether it beats the weakest member of that answer. A min-heap gives you that weakest member in O(1) and swaps it out in O(log k). A max-heap of all n items would also work, but it costs O(n) memory.

questions.prompt: Last Stone Weight needs the two heaviest stones on every turn. `heapq` up to Python 3.13 has only min-heap functions. What is the usual way to get a max-heap?

choices.text: Call `heapq.heapify(stones)` and then read from the end of the list
Push each weight as `-weight`, and negate again when you pop
Pass `reverse=True` to `heapq.heapify`
Call `heapq.nlargest(2, stones)` on the list each turn

questions.explanation: Negating the numbers turns the smallest item into the largest, so a min-heap of `-weight` pops the heaviest stone first. The end of a heap list isn't the largest item, and `heapify` has no `reverse` argument. `nlargest` each turn gives the right stones but rescans the whole list every time instead of costing O(log n). Python 3.14 adds `heappush_max`, `heappop_max` and `heapify_max`, which do this without negating.

questions.prompt: The priority-queue recipe in the `heapq` docs stores entries as `[priority, count, task]`, where `count` comes from `itertools.count()`. Why the count?

choices.text: It makes `heappush` run in O(1) instead of O(log n)
`heapq` only accepts entries that have exactly three fields
Without it, `heapq` would pop the largest priority first rather than the smallest
It settles ties, so tasks are never compared and equal priorities stay in order

questions.explanation: Tuples and lists compare field by field. With `(priority, task)`, two equal priorities make Python compare the tasks, which raises `TypeError` for types such as dicts. A unique, increasing count settles every tie first, so tasks are never compared and equal priorities come out in the order they were added. It doesn't change the cost of a push.

questions.prompt: K Closest Points to Origin: describe a heap solution that never holds more than k points. Which heap do you use, what is the key, and why don't you need a square root?

model_answer.summary: Keep a max-heap of size k keyed by squared distance (pushed as a negative number into `heapq`), and pop the farthest point whenever the heap grows past k.
key_points: The heap holds the k closest points so far, and its root is the farthest of them, so it is a max-heap by distance
With `heapq`, push `(-(x*x + y*y), x, y)` so the farthest point sits at `h[0]`, and pop when the size passes k
Squared distance `x*x + y*y` ranks points in the same order as the true distance, so no square root is needed
It runs in O(n log k) time and O(k) extra space
`heapq.nsmallest(k, points, key=lambda p: p[0]**2 + p[1]**2)` is a one-line alternative

questions.explanation: It is the top-k pattern turned around: to keep the k smallest distances, you evict the largest one, so the heap has to show you its maximum. `heapq` is a min-heap, so negate the key. Because the square root only grows as its input grows, comparing squared distances gives the same order and avoids floating-point work.
